Text features of test items

Source: R/ai-itemtext.R
item_features.Rd

Describes each item by features that can be read off its text before anyone answers it: How long and how hard to read the stem is, how many and how large its numbers are, whether it uses decimals or fractions or a negation, and, for multiple-choice items, what its options look like. It also finds each item's most similar other item, to flag near-duplicates. Everything runs in base R.

Usage

item_features(items, stem = "stem", options = NULL, key = "key", id = "id")

Arguments

items

a data frame with one row per item.

stem

name of the column that holds the stem (question text).

options

names of the option columns; NULL uses whichever of A to E exist. Use character(0) for items without options.

key

name of the column with the keyed option (a letter matching one of options); ignored when absent.

id

name of the item id column; when absent, items are numbered.

Value

A tibble with one row per item: id and the features above.

Details

The features are the item covariates of an explanatory IRT model such as the linear logistic test model (LLTM): Pass them with the items' difficulties to predict_difficulty(). They are deliberately simple and transparent. Your own features (an item writer's rating of the number of solution steps, or text embeddings from a language model) can be joined by id and used in the same way.

The features are:

  • words, sentences: Words (including numbers) and sentences in the stem.

  • word_length: Mean letters per word.

  • grade: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of the stem, from words per sentence and syllables per word.

  • numbers, max_digits: How many numbers the stem contains, and the digits in the whole part of the largest one.

  • decimals: 1 if the stem or the keyed option uses decimals or fractions (whole amounts of money such as $5.00 do not count).

  • negation: 1 if the stem contains not, never, no, except, least or false.

  • option_words: Mean words per option.

  • key_longest: 1 if the keyed option is longer than every other option, a classic item-writing flaw.

  • distractor_distance: For numeric options, the median distance of the distractors from the key, relative to the key (NA when the options are not all numbers). Close distractors usually make an item harder.

  • option_overlap: Mean word overlap (Jaccard) between pairs of options.

  • similarity, nearest: The overlap (Jaccard) of the two-word sequences in the item's stem and options with those of its most similar other item, and that item's id. Values near 1 mark near-duplicates; items written from the same template with different numbers score lower, because every changed number breaks two sequences.

See also

predict_difficulty() to predict difficulty from the features; the AI Hub.

Examples

f <- item_features(itemtext)
f
#> # A tibble: 192 × 15
#>    id     words sentences word_length grade numbers max_digits decimals negation
#>    <chr>  <int>     <int>       <dbl> <dbl>   <int>      <int>    <int>    <int>
#>  1 N01-01    13         2        3.91   0.9       2          2        0        0
#>  2 N01-02    21         3        4.05   0.8       2          2        0        0
#>  3 N01-03    21         3        3.79   2         2          2        0        0
#>  4 N01-04    13         2        3.91   0.9       2          2        0        0
#>  5 N01-05    13         2        3.91   0.9       2          2        0        0
#>  6 N01-06    21         3        4.05   0.8       2          2        0        0
#>  7 N01-07    13         2        3.91   0.9       2          2        0        0
#>  8 N01-08    13         2        3.91   0.9       2          2        0        0
#>  9 N01-09    20         3        3.78   1.4       2          1        1        0
#> 10 N01-10    13         2        3.91   0.9       2          2        1        0
#> # ℹ 182 more rows
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: option_words <dbl>, key_longest <int>,
#> #   distractor_distance <dbl>, option_overlap <dbl>, similarity <dbl>,
#> #   nearest <chr>
# surface features and difficulty
round(cor(f[, c("words", "max_digits", "decimals")], itemtext$b), 2)
#>             [,1]
#> words       0.00
#> max_digits -0.11
#> decimals    0.14
# the most similar pairs of items
head(f[order(-f$similarity), c("id", "nearest", "similarity")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   id     nearest similarity
#>   <chr>  <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 N01-02 N01-14       0.92 
#> 2 N01-14 N01-02       0.92 
#> 3 N06-05 N06-12       0.867
#> 4 N06-12 N06-05       0.867
#> 5 N08-01 N08-04       0.613
#> 6 N08-02 N08-11       0.613
